ECE 6612

Denial of service and resource budgets

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows incoming attack work crossing a limited link and a server delaying state allocation with a SYN cookie.

Availability means users can obtain a service when needed. A denial-of-service (DoS) attack interrupts that access through a flaw or by consuming a needed resource. Distributed DoS (DDoS) draws on many sending systems. A link, packet-processing engine, request queue, CPU or connection table can become the bottleneck. Identify the resource and its capacity before choosing a defense.

Let R be the counted bit rate in bits per second and L the counted bytes per packet. Packet rate is P = R/(8L) packets per second. A fixed bit rate generates more packet-handling work when packets are smaller. State which headers and link overhead are counted; mixing a payload-only size with a wire bit rate gives an inconsistent estimate. Fig. 2 lets the offered load and packet size change under an explicitly simplified resource model.

Filtering can discard traffic with known source or format patterns. Source spoofing forges an address; distribution adds actual senders. These complicate separating attack traffic from legitimate use. Filtering must occur while capacity remains: a host filter drops packets only after they have already crossed its access link. Source-address validation near sending networks reduces the set of addresses attackers can forge.

A TCP SYN flood can consume half-open connection state. A SYN-cookie server encodes recoverable setup information plus an integrity check into its SYN-ACK initial sequence number c, using a secret and freshness information. It keeps no ordinary per-SYN half-open record for that response. A completing client returns ACK = c+1; the server validates the returned information before allocating the established connection. A blind off-path sender with a forged source generally cannot observe the SYN-ACK needed to complete that proof. Cookie design, negotiated features and implementation details constrain the technique.

Reflection sends a request with the victim’s forged source address to an intermediary, which replies to the victim. If the counted response is Bᵣ bytes and request Bq bytes, byte amplification A = Bᵣ/Bq. Under the same counting convention, an attacker request rate r bit/s can induce approximately Ar bit/s of replies when the reflectors have capacity. Amplification in bytes and amplification in packet count are separate measures. Disabling exposed reflectors, rate limiting, source validation and upstream capacity address different stages.

A content-delivery or mitigation network can spread service and absorb or filter traffic upstream, subject to its capacity and application design. Protecting a SYN state table still leaves link and CPU limits to evaluate. A network telescope observes traffic sent to unused addresses, including victim replies to randomly spoofed attack sources. For an IPv4 /p telescope, the address-space fraction is f = 2^(32-p)/2^32 = 2^(-p). With uniform independent spoofing, one reply per triggering packet and no observation loss, a measured m replies/s estimates a total reply rate m/f. Selection biases, losses and different response counts change that inference.

Example

A 24 Mbit/s counted stream using 600-byte packets has P = 24,000,000/(8 × 600) = 5,000 packets/s. Under matching byte accounting, reflectors answering each 80-byte request with 1,200 bytes give A = 15. A /10 telescope covers 1/1,024 of IPv4, so 90 identified backscatter replies/s estimate 92,160 total replies/s under the stated random-source, one-response and loss-free assumptions.

Practice

1. An access link carries 12 Mbit/s of counted traffic. Compare 1,500-byte and 100-byte packets, ignoring additional overhead. Which count changes, and why might a SYN cookie still leave this link saturated?

Convert bytes to bits for each packet; then identify the resource protected by delayed state allocation.

The rates are 12,000,000/(8 × 1,500) = 1,000 packets/s and 12,000,000/(8 × 100) = 15,000 packets/s. Small packets create fifteen times as many handling events at the same bit rate. A SYN cookie protects half-open connection-state allocation; the incoming packets still consume access-link capacity.

2. A /12 IPv4 telescope observes 35 identifiable backscatter replies per second. Estimate the total reply rate under uniform independent source spoofing, one response per triggering packet and no losses. Which assumption would a reflector attack with the fixed victim source violate?

Compute the telescope’s address fraction and identify where replies are addressed.

A /12 has fraction 1/4,096. The estimate is 35 × 4,096 = 143,360 replies/s. A reflection attack using one victim’s fixed source sends replies to that victim rather than uniformly scattered addresses, violating the uniform-source sampling assumption for this inference.
